standard_prerequisites.name: Cauchy condition for a sequence
standard_prerequisites.statement: A sequence x : N -> RD is Cauchy when the displayed epsilon-condition holds for all sufficiently large indices.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the hypothesis, referred to through the retained equation's label.

standard_prerequisites.name: Countable choice for properties of natural numbers
standard_prerequisites.statement: A suitable choice principle converts the pointwise Cauchy condition into a modulus.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the retained result invoked at source line 552 to produce M.

standard_prerequisites.name: Cauchy completeness of the Dedekind reals
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every Cauchy approximation of Dedekind reals has a limit.
standard_prerequisites.use: It produces y at source lines 553-554.

core_obligations: Apply the retained choice principle to the Cauchy condition to obtain a modulus M such that xbar(epsilon) := x_{M(epsilon/2)} is a Cauchy approximation (source line 552).
Let y be the limit of xbar, which exists by the retained completeness theorem (source lines 553-554).
For a given epsilon choose n := M(epsilon/4) and estimate |x_m - y| for m >= n by splitting through x_n and using the triangle inequality (source lines 554-560).
Conclude the displayed convergence statement with the estimate epsilon/4 + epsilon/2 + epsilon/4 = epsilon (source lines 557-561).

proof_roadmap.step: Choice gives the modulus and completeness gives the limit.
The triangle-inequality estimate and the conclusion.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the unlabelled corollary at source lines 542-549, original Corollary 11.2.10: a Cauchy sequence of Dedekind reals converges in the classical epsilon-N formulation. The author's proof (source lines 551-562) is short but it consumes three separate inputs and finishes with an explicit estimate: a choice principle converts the pointwise Cauchy condition into a modulus M and a Cauchy approximation xbar (line 552), completeness of the Dedekind reals supplies the limit y (lines 553-554), and the convergence estimate for m >= n is then obtained by inserting x_n and applying the triangle inequality to reach epsilon/4 + epsilon/2 + epsilon/4 = epsilon (lines 554-561). The statement records only the classical formulation; the modulus and the intermediate point are invisible in it.
